subsystems.name: Magnetic field source
subsystems.role: creates a dipole field large enough to stand off the solar wind upstream of Mars.

subsystems.name: Plasma torus generator
subsystems.role: alternative approach: a cloud of ionised gas held in place, whose currents produce a protective field.

subsystems.name: L1 station platform
subsystems.role: keeps the field source positioned between Mars and the Sun.

subsystems.name: Diagnostics and monitoring
subsystems.role: measures whether the field actually deflects the solar wind and reduces escape.

subsystems.name: Mars atmosphere system
subsystems.role: the target being protected: the planet's thin CO2 atmosphere and its radiation environment.

buildSteps.title: Measure today's escape
buildSteps.detail: Orbiters such as NASA's MAVEN and ESA's Mars Express quantify how much atmosphere Mars loses to the solar wind, giving a baseline.

buildSteps.title: Model the shield
buildSteps.detail: Simulations test how a dipole field or plasma torus at Mars–Sun L1 would reshape the solar wind and the induced magnetotail.

buildSteps.title: Choose the field source
buildSteps.detail: Engineers compare a superconducting coil — compact but power-hungry — with a plasma torus, which is lighter but harder to control.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate in space
buildSteps.detail: A small version is flown in Earth orbit or lunar orbit to test deployment, cryogenics and plasma generation.

buildSteps.title: Fly a precursor to Mars L1
buildSteps.detail: A modest shield is stationed at L1 to measure solar-wind deflection and radiation reduction at Mars.

buildSteps.title: Scale up and operate
buildSteps.detail: A full-size field source is assembled and kept running for decades, with redundant power and station-keeping.

buildSteps.title: Watch the atmosphere respond
buildSteps.detail: Surface pressure, escape rate and radiation are monitored over many years to see whether the atmosphere begins to accumulate.

prerequisites.why: high-temperature superconductors exist, but coils tens of kilometres across have never been flown or deployed.

prerequisites.tech: Space nuclear power or very large solar arrays
prerequisites.why: a magnetic shield needs continuous megawatt-scale power far from Earth.
the shield and its power source are too large for a single launch.
decades of Mars orbiter data and global simulations give a working picture of atmospheric loss.
models disagree on how quickly an atmosphere would build up once escape is reduced.
laboratory and simulation work exists, but no one has controlled a plasma structure thousands of kilometres wide.

pathway.milestone: continue measuring Mars atmospheric escape with orbiters
pathway.unlocks: a firm baseline for judging whether any shield works.

pathway.milestone: small-scale in-space demonstration of a deployable magnetic shield
pathway.unlocks: confidence that the hardware can survive launch and operate autonomously.
direct measurements of solar-wind deflection and radiation reduction at Mars.
atmospheric retention and a safer radiation environment, though thickening the air would still take centuries.
a Mars that holds its own air — a speculative end point, not a near-term engineering project.
